text:
State of Stock: Based on this updated assessment, the Acadian Redfish (Sebastes fasciatus) stock is not
overfished and overfishing is not occurring (Figures 1-2). Retrospective adjustments were made to the model results for the purpose of stock status determination. Retrospective adjusted spawning stock biomass (SSB) in 2024 was estimated to be 188,005 (mt) which is 143% of the biomass target (SSBM SY proxy of SSB at F50% = 131,411;
Projections: Short term projections of total fishery yield and SSB for Acadian Redfish were conducted in
WHAM, using a harvest scenario of fishing at the FM SY proxy between 2026 and 2028. Catch in 2025 was estimated at 4,616 (mt) by the NEFMC Groundfish Plan Development Team. Recruitments were based on the average of estimated age-1 recruitment between 1969 and 2022, and the associated uncertainty in the recruitment
process, which is propagated in the projections by WHAM. The annual fishery selectivity, natural mortality, maturity ogive, and mean weights used in projections are the same as those used in the assessment model. Retrospective adjusted SSB and fully selected F in 2024 fell outside the 90% confidence intervals of the unadjusted 2024 values. The WHAM does not include the option to use Mohn’s rho values to make retrospective adjustments to projected fishery yield and SSB (see the special comments section for more details). Therefore, the unadjusted short term projection results are reported here.
Special Comments:
 What are the most important sources of uncertainty in this stock assessment? Explain, and describe qualitatively how they affect the assessment results (such as estimates of biomass, F, recruitment, and population projections). One of the primary sources of uncertainty in the Acadian Redfish assessment is the lack of age data, from the commercial fishery and spring survey. Although age samples were collected, they were not processed after 1985 due to the relatively low levels of fishery landings. As a result, the fall survey remains the only continuous source of age data for the assessment. This gap has required mean weight-at-age, maturity, and fishery selectivity to be held constant over time, which is unlikely to reflect reality. For Acadian Redfish in particular, holding mean weight-at-age constant ignores potential cohort-driven growth variation, while holding maturity constant fails to capture possible density-dependent shifts in reproductive schedules. These assumptions introduce potential model misspecification that can propagate into estimates of F, recruitment, and SSB, and contribute to the retrospective pattern observed in the assessment. The NEFSC Age and Growth Lab restarted the processing of fishery and spring survey age samples in the late 2010s, after fishery catches had returned to 1985 levels. Since 2020, the NEFSC Age and Growth Lab has worked to process archived age samples from the fishery and spring survey, in addition to the new years of age samples, but gaps in the age composition data still remain. The other primary source of uncertainty in the Acadian Redfish assessment is the lack of model fit to the spring and fall survey indices in recent assessments. Both the spring and fall survey indices show a decline in relative abundance in recent years. The previous ASAP model had difficulty fitting these declines, due to the relatively low natural (M = 0.05) and fishing (F < 0.05) mortality rates during that time period. As new years of lower index values were added, the ASAP model would split the difference between the higher index values prior to the decline and the lower values following the decline, which would pull the SSB estimates at the end of the assessment time series lower with each successive assessment. This model behavior is a likely contributor to the assessment’s retrospective pattern. While the WHAM used in this assessment improves the fit to both the spring and fall survey indices, it still fails the fit the most recent two years of the fall survey index, which are the lowest index values since the index began increasing in the mid-1990s. The plan for the next Acadian Redfish assessment is to explore the use of numbers at age (NAA) transition random effects in the WHAM. If NAA transition random effects are included in the model, this would likely lead to further improvements in the fit to the survey indices, which could change our perception of the stock.
 Does this assessment model have a retrospective pattern? If so, is the pattern minor, or major? (A major retrospective pattern occurs when the adjusted SSB or FF ull lies outside of the approximate joint confidence region for SSB and FF ull ). This assessment has a major retrospective pattern in SSB and F. Retrospective adjusted SSB (Mohn’s rho = 0.155) and fully selected F (Mohn’s rho = -0.130) in 2024 fell outside the 90% confidence intervals of the unadjusted 2024 values. It should be noted that this major retrospective pattern is due more to the tight confidence intervals produced by the model, than to particularly high Mohn’s rho values for SSB and fully selected F. A retrospective adjustment to the terminal year SSB and fully selected F was used for the purpose of stock
status determination, but not for short term projections. For reference, retrospective adjusted terminal year
SSB was 13% less than the unadjusted value, and retrospective adjusted terminal year fully selected F was 15% greater than the unadjusted value. The WHAM does not include an option to use Mohn’s rho values to make retrospective adjustments to projected fishery yield and SSB. Work was done to develop a post hoc approach to manually adjust projected fishery yield and SSB, but a generalized approach could not be found.  Based on this stock assessment, are population projections well determined or uncertain? If this stock is in a rebuilding plan, how do the projections compare to the rebuilding schedule? Due to the retrospective pattern described in the first two special comments, projected SSB from the previous assessment tends to be higher than the estimated SSB for the same years from this assessment. The Acadian Redfish stock is not in a rebuilding plan.  Describe any changes that were made to the current stock assessment, beyond incorporating additional years of data and the effect these changes had on the assessment and stock status. Four years of historic fishery age composition data and three years of historic spring survey age composition data were added to the assessment. The 2023 spring survey index value was treated as missing data, because only 1 of the 11 survey strata normally included in the index was towed in 2023. The assessment start year was changed from 1913 to 1963 (i.e., the first year of survey data), becasue the model had difficulty estimating age-1 recruitment in the earlier years, when only aggregated catch data were available. The fishery and survey age composition likelihood components were changed from multinomial distributions to logistic-normal distributions with 0 values treated as missing data and a first-order autoregressive process. This change in likelihood components eliminated the positive bias in one step ahead (OSA) residuals for the fishery and survey age composition data. The recruitment model was changed from a Beverton-Holt model with IID random effects to a mean recruitment model with AR1 random effects. The Beverton-Holt model was effectively estimating a steepness of 1, and changing to the mean recruitment model improved model parsimony, while producing similar results. The equilibrium initial NAA model, which was already being used in the WHAM, remained the best initial NAA model, based on AIC. The other initial NAA models did not perform as well, likely due to the assessment including 26 ages for which the model had to estimate either fixed effect parameters or random effects. Fishery and survey selectivity were changed from logistic functions to age-specific selectivity parameters. The increased flexibility of the age-specific parameters produced better fits to the age composition data.  If the stock status has changed a lot since the previous assessment, explain why this occurred. There has been no change in the stock status of Acadian Redfish since the previous assessment. In addition, stock status was insensitive to whether or not a retrospective adjustment was applied to the terminal year SSB and fully selected F estimates.  Provide qualitative statements describing the condition of the stock that relate to stock status. Total fishery removals of Acadian Redfish have been relatively constant since the 2010s. At the same time, the spring and fall survey indices have shown a decrease in relative abundance, which the previous ASAP model struggled to fit. The current WHAM improves the fit to the survey indices, which results in the stock being estimated as less productive than previous assessments suggested. While the stock status has not changed from the last assessment, the terminal year estimates of SSB and fully selected F are closer to the SSB and F
thresholds than in previous assessments. If model fits to the indices are further improved in the future, then our perception of the stock and its productivity may continue to change.  Indicate what data or studies are currently lacking and which would be needed most to improve this stock assessment in the future. The Acadian Redfish assessment could be improved by filling more of the gaps in the fishery and spring survey age compositions. To this end, the NEFSC Age and Growth Lab has been continuing its efforts to process historical age samples. One of the hypotheses to explain the decrease in the spring and fall survey indices is that some fish have moved into Canadian waters. A genetic study of Acadian Redfish in U.S. and Canadian waters might be one way to test this hypothesis. Such a study could be coupled with a comparison of U.S. and Canadian survey trends and associated length distributions.  Are there other important issues? While the WHAM used in this assessment improves the fit to both the spring and fall survey indices, it still fails to fit the most recent two years of the fall survey index, which are the lowest index values since the index began increasing in the mid-1990s. The plan for the next Acadian Redfish assessment is to continue to improve the WHAM and explore the use of NAA transition random effects in the model. If NAA transition random effects are included in the model, this would likely lead to further improvements in the fit to the survey indices, which could change our perception of the stock. The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) recently initiated a plan to purchase USD 20 million worth of groundfish, with a focus on Pollock, Haddock, and Acadian Redfish (USDA 2025). The USDA’s plan could encourage increased targeting of Acadian Redfish at a time when indices are showing a decrease in relative abundance. This is another factor that could lead to a change in our perception of the stock at the next assessment.

meta.stock_name: Acadian redfish - Gulf of Maine / Georges Bank

text:
State of Stock: Based on this management track assessment, the Northwest Atlantic Mackerel (Scomber
scombrus) stock is not overfished and overfishing is not occurring (Figures 1-2). Retrospective patterns were minor and retrospective adjustments for terminal year estimates were not needed. Spawning stock biomass (SSB) in 2024 was estimated to be 94,702 (mt), corresponding to 56% of the biomass target (SSBM SY proxy = 169,139; Figure 1). The 2024 fully selected fishing mortality was estimated to be 0.04, corresponding to 20% of the overfishing threshold proxy (FM SY proxy = 0.2; Figure 2).
Projections: Following the established Rebuilding 2.0 Amendment (MAFMC 2023), short-term projections were
derived assuming two recruitment stanzas. When projected SSB for a given iteration was less than of SSBM SY
proxy, recruitment was derived by sampling from a cumulative distribution function of recruitment estimates from 2009 onward from the final ASAP model; when projected SSB for a given iteration was greater than or equal to of SSBM SY proxy, recruitment was dervied by sampling from a cumulative distribution function of recruitment estimates from 1975 onward. The annual fishery selectivity, maturity ogive, and mean weights-at-age used in the projections represent the most recent 5-year averages.
Special Comments:
 What are the most important sources of uncertainty in this stock assessment? Explain, and describe qualitatively how they affect the assessment results (such as estimates of biomass, F, recruitment, and population projections). While the CV of the terminal year (2024) recruitment estimate is only 44%, this estimate is solely informed by the 2024 fishery age composition data and is therefore comparatively uncertain. In previous assessments that indicated a strong terminal year recruitment, the estimated magnitude of the year class was revised downward in subsequent assessments. An overestimation of terminal year recruitment could result in an overestimation of SSB and overly optimistic short-term projections. To create a range-wide index of spawning stock biomass, SSB estimates developed from Canada’s dedicated egg survey and the U.S.’s ecosystem surveys are used. However, gonadosomatic index (GSI) estimates are not available for the southern contingent because the primary U.S. fishery does not overlap with the spawning season and the seasonal bottom trawl surveys occur before or after the spawning season. Consequently, an average spawning seasonality function was used to calculate annual egg production. Similarly, due to a lack of fecundity estimates for the southern contingent, annual fecundity estimates from the Gulf of St. Lawrence were used to calculate spawning stock biomass from annual egg production. Together these assumptions introduce uncertainty in SSB estimates of the southern contingent and therefore, contingent contributions. Canadian catch estimates represent a subset of total Canadian catch because bait fishery, recreational fishery and commercial discard estimates are not available. Uncertainty in removals can impact the magnitude of estimated fishing mortality and biomass estimates. Consistent with previous assessments, natural mortality (M) is assumed to be constant over both time and age. To consider evidence of different natural mortality rates, a likelihood profile was updated for this assessment and supports the assumed value. Ongoing work with Canada’s Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) and the ICES Working Group of Northwest Atlantic Mackerel (WGNAM) on the development of life history-based estimates of M and a Predation Pressure Index (Richards and Jacobson 2016) may enable a reevaluation of the natural mortality assumption used in the model. Additionally, further development of a WHAM model would enable the exploration of time and age-varying processes, such as natural mortality, in the model.  Does this assessment model have a retrospective pattern? If so, is the pattern minor, or major? (a major
retrospective pattern occurs when the adjusted SSB or FF ull lies outside of the approximate joint confidence region for SSB and FF ull ): The 5-year Mohn’s ρ, relative to SSB, was 0.485 in the 2023 assessment (terminal year of 2022) and 0.305 in this assessment (terminal year of 2024). The 5-year Mohn’s ρ, relative to F, was -0.306 in the 2023 assessment (terminal year of 2022) and -0.201 in this assessment (terminal year of 2024). The retrospective pattern for this assessment was considered to be minor because the ρ-adjusted estimates of 2024 SSB (SSBρ =72566) and 2024 F (Fρ =0.053) were within the approximate 90% confidence intervals around SSB (52,539 - 170,702) and F (0.021 - 0.076). Consequently, a retrospective adjustment of spawning stock biomass or fishing mortality in 2024 was not required. While the retrospective pattern was considered to be minor, the retrospective analysis indicated a consistent underestimation of fishing mortality and overestimation of SSB, though less severe than that from the 2023 management track.  Based on this stock assessment, are population projections well determined or uncertain? If this stock is in a rebuilding plan, how do the projections compare to the rebuilding schedule? Past assessments for this stock have demonstrated high uncertainty in short-term projections where projected increases in SSB were subsequently not realized. The 2017 benchmark projected an SSB of approximately 162,800 mt for 2019, but this estimate was revised downward in subsequent assessments to approximately 42,800 mt (2021 MT) and 23,500 mt (2023 MT). In constrast, the 2025 MT indicates that the increase in 2023-2024 SSB projected by the last assessment and resulting rebuilding schedule was realized or exceeded. Differences in projection performance in part reflect differences in realized versus assumed year class strength; for 2017-2021, realized recruitment was less than the projected median values, whereas for 2022-2024, estimated recruitment was at or above the projected median values. Similar to the 2017 benchmark and 2023 management track assessments, short-term projections are driven by a strong incoming cohort (2023 year class). The 2015 and 2021 year classes, while still above the time-series median, are now approximately 30% and 23% lower than their terminal year estimates from the 2017 and 2023 assessments, respectively. DFO Canada’s recent assessment of the northern spawning contingent estimated weak 2021-2023 year classes (DFO 2025). However, recent US and Canadian egg data indicated that the southern contingent’s contribution to stock-level estimates of SSB increased to a time series high of 81% in 2024, potentially contributing to contingent-specific differences in recruitment.  Describe any changes that were made to the current stock assessment, beyond incorporating additional years of data and the effect these changes had on the assessment and stock status. NEFSC spring bottom trawl survey indices were updated due to minor changes in the assumed length-weight relationship. This update had a negligible impact on the survey time series and resulting model estimates. U.S. commercial catch estimates were updated for 2020-2022 using the CAMS database, which resulted in a minor (less than 12%) increase in F and decrease in SSB in recent years. The 2022 egg index value was updated due to a change in the assumed fecundity estimate, and the 2020-2022 weight-at-age (WAA) estimates used to calculate SSB for the egg index were also updated due to changes in the catch WAA. Both of these changes had negligible impacts on resulting model estimates.  If the stock status has changed a lot since the previous assessment, explain why this occurred. The stock status of Northwest Atlantic Mackerel has changed since the previous assessment (NEFSC 2023). While overfishing is still not occurring, the stock is no longer considered to be overfished, though it is not yet rebuilt. This change in overfished status is likely due to the closure of the Canadian directed commercial fishery and low U.S. removals in recent years, as well as recent recruitment estimates (2022-2024) above the time-series median.  Provide qualitative statements describing the condition of the stock that relate to stock status. Fishery composition data show a truncation in age structure, primarily during the 2010s. Age-9 fish were observed in 2019-2024 catches for the first time since 2012, however, age-7+ fish represent less than 1% of total removals. After being near a time-series minimum in 2022, the egg survey increased approximately three-fold from 2022 to 2023, and then decreased 25% in 2024. Compared to the previous decade, egg
production of the southern contingent has been an order of magnitude greater since 2018, and the proportion of the index represented by the southern contingent reached a time series high of 81% in 2024.  Indicate what data or studies are currently lacking and which would be needed most to improve this stock assessment in the future. As mentioned in the above section on sources of uncertainty, fecundity estimates for the southern contingent are needed to improve spawning stock biomass estimates developed from the egg surveys. Additionally, further work is needed to explore both the magnitude and temporal variation in natural mortality as an incorrect characterization of natural mortality, if truly changing over time, could contribute to a retrospective pattern and impact short-term projection performance. Further work on stock structure and the extent of contingent mixing is also needed. Otolith natal isotopic compositions have been shown to shift over time (Arai et al. 2021) and contingent mixing, as well as contingent contributions to catches, can vary among year classes (Redding et al. 2020, Arai et al. 2021). Consequently, in order to develop spatially-explicit assessment models that consider the dynamics of each spawning contingent separately, year-class-specific baselines and annual estimates of contingent composition in fishery catches would be needed. Recent genetic work (Bourretet al 2023) has indicated small, but potentially significant genetic differentiation between the two spawning contingents; however, improvements in the reference samples used for the southern contingent are needed to minimize potential bias in contingent assignments and further investigate whether the southern continent is present in Canadian waters during late spring to autumn.  Are there other important issues? DFO Canada’s 2025 assessment of the northern spawning contingent of northwest Atlantic mackerel (DFO 2025) indicated that the northern contingent has been in or near the Critical Zone, as defined by DFO’s precautionary approach framework, since 2011. Estimated spawning stock biomass reached a time-series minimum in 2022 (9,965 mt at the time of spawning) and increased slightly during 2023-2024, but still remained at only 35% of the limit reference point in 2024. Estimated fishing mortality for fully selected fish (age-5+) has been below F40% since 2022. Estimated recruitment has been below the time-series median since 2009 with the last notable recruitment event in 2016. In contrast to the recruitment values estimated in this management track assessment, the 2022-2024 recruitment estimates from DFO’s assessment represented the third to fifth lowest estimates of the time series.

meta.stock_name: Atlantic mackerel - Gulf of Maine / Cape Hatteras

text:
State of Stock: Based on the results of this management track assessment, the Black Sea Bass (Centropristis
striata) stock is not overfished and overfishing is not occurring (Figures 1-2). Spawning stock biomass (SSB) in 2024 was estimated to be 30,896 (mt) which is 284% of the biomass target (SSBM SY proxy = 10,877; Figure 1). The 2024 fully selected fishing mortality was estimated to be 0.75 which is 73% of the overfishing threshold proxy (FM SY proxy = 1.036; Figure 2).
Projections: Short term (three year) projections were conducted in WHAM, which propagates uncertainty in
fleet selectivity, numbers at age, and environmental covariates. For projection specifications, predicted recruitment was averaged for years after 1999 and the most recent 5-year average of age specific maturity, weight-at-age, fleet selectivity, and natural mortality estimates were used. The ABC catch was used in the first projection year followed by FM SY proxy in subsequent years.
Special Comments:
 What are the most important sources of uncertainty in this stock assessment? Explain, and describe qualitatively how they affect the assessment results (such as estimates of biomass, F, recruitment, and population projections). The recreational catch and the recreational catch-per-angler index both relied on data from the Marine Recreational Information Program (MRIP) which is planning a substantial re-calculation and evaluation in the next few years. To date, the MRIP estimates are a major source of uncertainty in stocks that use these data. Another source of uncertainty is the NEFSC bottom trawl survey data in spring 2023, which only surveyed on Georges Bank and therefore lacked index information for the Gulf of Maine, Southern New England, or the southern region between Hudson Canyon to Cape Hatteras. The bottom trawl survey is only one of several that inform the model-based index time series used in the assessment (VAST), but its spatial (area weighting = 0.8) and temporal (36 year) coverage make it highly influential. The VAST index value in the South for 2023 contributes to the upward trend in recent years. Sensitivity tests were done to exclude the VAST index for 2023 but the results did not change the stock status. Another source of uncertainty stemmed from the lack of length information on landings in the unclassified market category which have not been sampled in the North since 2020, and in the South since 2013. Calculating the catch at length for 2021-2024 necessitated borrowing information from before 2020 and across regions which introduces additional uncertainty.  Does this assessment model have a retrospective pattern? If so, is the pattern minor, or major? (A major retrospective pattern occurs when the adjusted SSB or FF ull lies outside of the approximate joint confidence region for SSB and FF ull ). The 7-year Mohn’s ρ, relative to SSB, was 0.01 in the North and -0.132 in the South in the 2024 assessment and was -0.066 in the North and -0.066 in the South in the current assessment. The 7-year Mohn’s ρ, relative to fully selected F, was 0.008 in the North and 0.1 in the South in the 2024 assessment and was 0.09 in the North and 0.023 in the South in the current assessment. There was not a major retrospective pattern for this assessment because the ρ adjusted estimates of 2024 SSB (SSBρ =33,087) and 2024 F (Fρ =0.7) were inside the approximate 90% confidence regions around SSB (22,609 - 48,655) and F (0.49 1.002). No retrospective adjustment of spawning stock biomass or fishing mortality in 2024 was required.  Based on this stock assessment, are population projections well determined or uncertain? If this stock is in a rebuilding plan, how do the projections compare to the rebuilding schedule? Population projections for Black Sea Bass are relatively well determined. The projected biomass from the 2024 management track assessment was within the 95% confidence bounds of the biomass estimated in the current assessment. Realized catch in 2024 was approximately the 2024 ABC that was used in short-term projections from the previous Management Track Assessment. While estimated SSB in the current assessment did not decline as projected by the 2024 Management Track Assessment model, it was within the uncertainty bounds of SSB for this model. This stock is not in a rebuilding plan.  Describe any changes that were made to the current stock assessment, beyond incorporating additional years of data and the effect these changes had on the assessment and stock status. The inter-year correlation of the 2DAR(1) numbers-at-age process error was decoupled, such that a
separate value was estimated for age-1 individuals and age 2+ individuals. Other than that, the only change to the model is the incorporation of 2024 data.  If the stock status has changed a lot since the previous assessment, explain why this occurred. The stock status of Black Sea Bass did not change since the previous assessment. Reference points are statistically the same as those of the previous assessment.  Provide qualitative statements describing the condition of the stock that relate to stock status. The Black Sea Bass stock shows recent strong levels of recruitment that have sustained a high spawning stock biomass in the North and have increased the spawning stock biomass in the South. This pattern influences the age structure in the North and South, with a more expanded age structure in the previous 10 years than is observed earlier in the time series.  Indicate what data or studies are currently lacking and which would be needed most to improve this stock assessment in the future. The Black Sea Bass assessment could be improved with sampling the length composition of the unclassified market category. Care should be taken to continue the existing sampling regime of the NEFSC Bottom Trawl survey as these data are an indispensable source of fisheries-independent information to inform abundance. Likewise, the portside sampling program provides essential length information of the commercial landings and if the volume of these data diminish, it would need to be supplemented by additional sampling programs.  Are there other important issues?
